abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.
authors: Daniel S. Han, Vaishnavi Ananthanarayanan, Matthew J. Simpson
title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters

abstract: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.

title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles

abstract: Medium-range order (MRO) is an important feature of amorphous materials, but its nature in terms of atomic arrangement has remained elusive. Here, using large-scale machine-learning-driven atomistic simulations of amorphous silicon, we probe the MRO of this archetypal network glass. By characterizing the structure in three dimensions, we reveal that the symmetry of the atomic arrangement around a central atom shows a crossover as a function of distance. At short distances, the structure is determined by local bonding constraints, which evolve from predominantly tetrahedral environments in low-density amorphous silicon to highly coordinated and strongly disordered local environments in very-high-density amorphous silicon. At larger distances, however, distinct cubic- and octahedral-symmetry patterns emerge in the three-dimensional atomic-density distribution, despite the absence of these symmetries at shorter length scales. We find that this crossover is accompanied by a quasi-periodic spatial organization of the topological rings in the structure. The characteristic spacing between ring centers matches the length scale of the first sharp diffraction peak (FSDP) in the structure factor, establishing a direct connection between this reciprocal-space signature of MRO and its real-space organization. These results demonstrate that the FSDP, the spatial correlation of the rings, and emergent orientational symmetries are not independent manifestations of MRO, but reflect different aspects of a common structural organization. Our findings provide a unified real-space picture of MRO in amorphous silicon and suggest that intermediate-range structural order in network glasses emerges from the interplay between local bonding constraints and extended atomic arrangements driven by efficient packing.
authors: Zhen Zhang, Stephen R. Elliott, Yujie Wang, Walter Kob
title: Emergent medium-range order in amorphous silicon

abstract: Binary active systems offer a minimal platform for understanding how component heterogeneity organizes non-equilibrium structures. Here we show that in a binary Quincke system driven by a periodic square-wave electric field, a dynamic square lattice in which small particles occupy the lattice-cell centers which are surrounded by large particles emerges spontaneously. Particle-resolved trajectories reveal that the size separation arises from the mobility difference of large particles and small particles. Increasing the driving frequency reduces the single-cycle path lengths of both species and simultaneously decreases the lattice constant. These results show how size-dependent activity,density redistribution, and periodic forcing cooperate to generate tunable complex active patterns.

abstract: Tangles of soft filaments are ubiquitous, from living worm blobs to the cables in a desk drawer. How do such tangles, held together by friction and entanglement, respond when one embedded filament is shaken? We suspend disordered tangles of tunable cohesion and ordered stitched meshes from a single thread (the tether) and oscillate it vertically at fixed amplitude. Extraction peaks at an intermediate drive frequency ($\sim 15$ Hz) and declines at higher frequencies, although the peak drive acceleration grows quadratically. Here we combine experiments, high-speed imaging, and a tension-only spring-mass model to show that this non-monotonic response is set by timing rather than resonance. The extraction window is bounded below by a slackening threshold, where the peak drive acceleration exceeds gravity and the tether, slack for part of each cycle, creates a tensile impulse each time it snaps taut. The window is bounded above by a transmission crossover, where the transmission time across the tangle exceeds a quarter of the drive cycle, so that the tangle no longer responds as a whole and the drive's work dissipates internally. The slackening threshold depends only on the drive and gravity, while the transmission crossover is set only by the tangle's size and transmission speed. By tracing extraction to the overlap of impulse creation and impulse transmission, we identify a generic principle of driven filamentous matter and suggest frequency-selective routes to its disassembly.
authors: Ishant Tiwari, Sutikshan Bansal, Rosalind Huang, Chenyi Fei, Jörn Dunkel, Vishal Patil, Saad Bhamla
title: Why shaking faster does not untangle: frequency-selective extraction of filaments from tangled matter

abstract: Quantifying the biological effects of radiation is essential for radiotherapy and radiation protection. While research has centered on statistical analyses of experimental data, this approach often fails to elucidate underlying mechanisms, limiting the development of generalizable models. Describing time dependent phenomena, such as sub-lethal damage (SLD) recovery during fractionated irradiation, presents a particularly significant challenge for existing static models. To address this, we developed a mechanistic mathematical model that extends the classical multi-target, single-hit model by introducing explicit recovery transitions among damage states, allowing the simultaneous description of radiation-induced damage accumulation and biological recovery. We applied this model to Elkind and Sutton's classical split-dose experimental data to determine its parameters. The model reproduced the major features of split-dose survival curves for treatments with 0-, 2.5-, and 23-hour recovery intervals. We visualized the temporal changes in damage state distributions within the cell populations. These simulations provided a process-level interpretation of the characteristic shoulder-like response appearing after an inter-fraction recovery interval. Furthermore, the estimated recovery half-life was about 120 minutes, which is broadly consistent with reported timescales of DNA double-strand break repair in mammalian cells, supporting the biological interpretability of the model parameters. The proposed framework provides a simple, interpretable description of radiation-induced cell death dynamics, including SLD recovery, and may serve as a basis for the improved mechanistic modeling of radiobiological effects under different irradiation protocols.

title: A dynamic mathematical model for sub-lethal damage recovery: Integrating recovery processes into multi-target theory to visualize damage states

abstract: Therapy resistance in glioblastoma is usually described in genetic or metabolic terms. Here we ask whether it also has a measurable biophysical form. Combining Raman spectroscopy with scanning acoustic microscopy on TRAIL-sensitive and TRAIL-resistant glioblastoma cells, we find that resistance carries both a biochemical and a mechanical signature: the resistant cells differ at protein, lipid and nucleic-acid bands, contain 4.1-fold more neutral lipid, and hold a high acoustic impedance that does not change when the drug is applied, while sensitive cells stiffen as they die. Because acoustic impedance is an absolute quantity and neither measurement requires a label, the approach offers a route to recognising resistant populations from their physical state alone.

abstract: The two prevalent methods to determine the position of individual fluorophores in the focal plane of a microscope rely either on the centroid of the fluorescence pattern produced by the fluorophore on a camera or on targeting the fluorophore's coordinate with a spatially controlled illumination minimum, as realized in MINFLUX. In both methods, (sub)nanometer localization precisions have been reached, but little is known about their accuracy, i.e., the deviation of the obtained coordinate from its ground truth. Here we report a theoretical and experimental comparison of the accuracy provided by these two strategies. We quantify substantial systematic errors in camera-based localization due to the interplay of two difficult-to-control parameters: the orientation of the fluorophore in space and its axial deviation from the focal plane (defocus). For example, within an axial range of {+/-}120 nm around the focus, the median distance between two fluorophores on a nanobody measured by camera-based localization varies by 26.5 nm. Under the same conditions, a commercial MINFLUX system yields a median variation in distance of 1.4 nm, indicating an improvement in accuracy by an order of magnitude. The accuracy of MINFLUX localization can be further improved to (sub-)[a]ngstrom levels by reducing the average distance between the coordinates targeted by the illumination minimum and the fluorophore. As it delivers unrivaled precision and accuracy for mapping fluorophores and their distances, we consider coordinate-targeted localization essential for studying labeled cells at the sub-10 nm level and for exploring structural and conformational changes of labeled biomolecules.

abstract: Like cholesterol, protein crowding has been shown to alter the temperature dependence of lateral diffusion in biomembranes, eventually eliminating the distinct liquid-gel phase transition. Here, we resolve the molecular origin of this protein effect with coarse-grained and all-atom simulations of protein-crowded phosphatidylcholine bilayers, which give access to lipid structure and dynamics on both sides of the transition temperature. Unlike cholesterol, which is known to induce a continuous liquid ordered phase by having opposite effects on the two phases, we find that membrane proteins decrease lipid order at all temperatures studied. The disordering is stronger at low temperatures, so that once the proteins cover roughly half of the membrane area the low- and high-temperature phases become alike and the transition is lost. Our results suggest that in addition to local cholesterol concentration, local protein concentration may also help dictate membrane fluidity and especially its response to temperature change.

title: Protein Crowding Buffers Membrane Fluidity

abstract: Characterizing how particles diffuse is key to understanding biology across scales, yet extracting the underlying physical properties typically requires specialized tools rarely accessible to biology labs. Here we introduce AnDi-J, a Fiji plugin combining classical estimators with state-of-the-art machine learning for single-trajectory analysis and segmentation, requiring minimal knowledge of stochastic processes. It extracts diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents, classifies trajectories into diffusion models, and segments heterogeneous trajectories into diffusive states, through powerful, easy-to-use visualization tools. See more at https://github.com/gorkamunoz/andi-j .

title: AnDi-J: diffusion analysis of single-particle tracking data in Fiji

abstract: Biomolecular condensation contributes to cellular organization and the regulation of numerous biochemical processes. Capturing its dynamics on large spatio-temporal scales requires a macroscopic model that accurately describes both thermodynamic forces and molecular transport. Here, we investigate the applicability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation for modeling phase-separation dynamics in intrinsically disordered proteins. Using the low-complexity domain of FUS as a model system for biomolecular condensation, we perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to infer the free-energy functional and mobility coefficient entering the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The resulting continuum model accurately describes the growth of initial concentration fluctuations in the spinodal regime and the subsequent morphological evolution of the concentration fields during coarsening. We find that the free-energy functional is transferable across different stages of phase separation, whereas the mobility is not. During coarsening, we identify two kinetic regimes characterized by distinct mobilities, which persist even when a concentration-dependent mobility is introduced.
authors: Hubman, A.; Potisk, T.; Merzel, F.
title: From coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to continuum models of biomolecular condensation

abstract: Centromeres must withstand high pulling forces in metaphase, yet allow rapid and complete chromosome segregation in anaphase. Using optical tweezers measurements on isolated human metaphase chromosomes, we find that centromeres are stiffer at low forces and more frequently exhibit pronounced softening compared to whole chromosomes, while displaying a similar stiffening response at high forces. We capture these mechanical properties by establishing a softened hierarchical worm-like chain model. Cohesin cleavage alters the mechanical properties of centromeres but does not lead to chromosome segregation in vitro. Topoisomerase II is recruited to centromeric regions under significant tension, likely to resolve the persistent centromeric DNA entanglements that provide additional sister chromatid cohesion. These findings advance our understanding of the mechanical resilience and regulation of centromeres during mitosis.

title: Mechanical characterization of human centromeres

abstract: Most fish species are ectothermic and rely on behavioral strategies to control their body temperature in heterothermal environments. Both thermotaxis and thermokinesis have been suggested as important underlying mechanisms. However, to what extent these behaviors allow fish to respond to rapid (timescales of minutes) and strong thermal disturbances, like those caused by anthropogenic water releases into natural freshwater systems, is poorly understood. Here, we quantify this response for a salmonid species with a novel laboratory approach coupled with image-based tracking. We exposed brown trout parr (Salmo trutta), acclimated to 12 °C, to rapidly forming cold- and warm-water interfaces with temperatures ranging from 4 to 20 °C. We found that fish actively avoided colder water (≤8 °C) through a rapid response that combined thermotaxis and thermokinesis. In contrast, fish did not avoid warmer water and frequently crossed interfaces having temperature contrasts of up to 8 °C. This study shows that brown trout parr swiftly deploy multiple behavioral strategies to minimize exposure to cold water and take advantage of warm water, illustrating their capability to cope with rapidly occurring thermal alterations.
authors: Jonasz Slomka, Luiz GM Silva, Markus Holzner, Robert M Boes, Robert Naudascher, Roman Stocker, Stefano Brizzolara
title: Salmonids elicit an acute behavioral response to heterothermal environments

abstract: Phase separation of two phase separating solutes in a common solvent can result in mesoscale (micron-sized) droplets with complex topologies of the domains of each solute within each droplet. Such topologies have been observed in vitro in systems of chromatin oligomers, biomolecular condensates, and polymeric mixtures. In these systems, the solutes phase separate from the solvent into droplets; within each droplet, further phase separation can occur between the two solutes. In some systems, the extent of demixing can be modulated by an additional molecular component. The minimal free energy topologies are predicted as universal functions of the interfacial tension ratios and fractions of each solute within a droplet. We compare the theoretically predicted droplet topologies with those reported in several experimental systems and discuss how the predicted topologies vary with the tensions. Experimental aspects that may depend on the kinetics or molecular weight variations in the system are also discussed.
authors: Kumar, Amit, Karpen, Gary, Safran, Samuel A.
title: Complex topologies in phase separated droplets predicted from universal phase diagram

abstract: The envelope glycoprotein (Env) of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) plays important roles in viral entry by coordinating host-cell receptor recognition and membrane fusion. Env is synthesized as a homotrimeric precursor, gp160, which is cleaved into gp120 and gp41 subunits. Although the cleaved form of Env is required for fusion, uncleaved Env remains plentiful on the surface of HIV-1-infected cells. Previous studies have suggested that uncleaved Env is conformationally more flexible than the cleaved form making its dynamics important for understanding the broader structural landscape of HIV-1 Env. In this study, we employed microsecond-long all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the dynamics of two structures of uncleaved HIV-1 Env that have been previously assigned to the same conformational state. Our results reveal differences in their conformational behavior, including differences in collective motions, FRET distributions, and trimer symmetry. These findings provide molecular-level insight into the structural plasticity of uncleaved HIV-1 Env and highlight that different structures within the same conformational state can exhibit distinct dynamic behavior.
authors: Sauve, S.; Moradi, M.
title: Differential Behavior of Uncleaved gp160 Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1) Envelope (Env) Glycoproteins

abstract: Two key factors required for pre-mRNA 3' end processing, CPSF73 and PCF11, are linked to poor cancer prognosis, yet their oncogenic roles remain unclear due to their dual function in transcription termination. Using a colorectal cancer (CRC) progression model, we show that primary tumor cells depend on high CPSF73 and PCF11 levels, whereas metastatic cells are less sensitive. This dependency is not explained by alternative polyadenylation (APA) or transcription-replication conflicts. Instead, we identify an uncoupling of 3' cleavage and transcription termination during CRC progression. Primary tumor cells exhibit a global shift toward proximal termination alongside distal APA usage, while metastatic cells partially revert to normal termination patterns and favor proximal APA. Notably, the distance between 3' cleavage and termination is nearly halved in primary tumor cells compared with normal cells and becomes particularly short in oncogenes. Reduced cleavage-termination distance correlates with increased gene expression both within and across cell states. These findings identify a previously unrecognized link between transcription termination architecture and gene expression regulation.

abstract: Fusion oncoproteins drive aggressive leukemias by mediating aberrant gene expression within specialized biomolecular condensates that contain various biomolecules. While RNA is known to influence condensate properties, the RNA constituents of fusion protein-containing onco-condensates remain poorly defined. Here, we use bicon-seq (biotinylated-isoxazole-mediated precipitation of condensome and RNA sequencing) to globally profile condensate-associated RNAs from cellular samples. Using experimental perturbation of cytoplasmic RNA-containing condensates, we demonstrated that bicon-seq accurately quantifies changes in RNA solubility, that correlate with published RNA enrichment in these structures. In leukemia cells driven by the NUP98::KDM5A fusion oncoprotein, bicon-seq revealed highly conserved long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) that are associated with NUP98::KDM5A onco-condensates. Among them, the lncRNA Gas5 was highly expressed and essential for the proliferation of AML cells. Mechanistically, Gas5 co-localized with NUP98::KDM5A in condensates and modulated NUP98::KDM5A chromatin binding and the expression dynamics of differentiation/apoptosis-associated genes in AML cells. Together, our results introduce a novel approach to systematically profile condensate-associated RNAs and identify the lncRNA Gas5 as a critical regulator of NUP98::KDM5A-driven transcription in AML cells.

abstract: Diabetes alters shape and deformability of red blood cells (RBCs), thereby potentially modifying their transport through capillary networks. However, the contribution of altered RBC biomechanics to network-scale changes in capillary hemodynamics and the cellular-scale mechanisms underlying such changes remain poorly understood. Current in vivo imaging techniques cannot directly quantify critical hemodynamic parameters including endothelial mechanical load, capillary pressure, and the cell-free layer in vessels less than 10 microns in diameter.

abstract: Rare events, such as crystal nucleation in mildly supercooled liquids, are characterized by waiting times that can be much longer than the timescale of the underlying microscopic dynamics. The mean first-passage time (MFPT) formalism [J. Wedekind and D. Reguera, J. Phys. Chem. B 112, 11060 (2008)] provides a route to reconstruct one-dimensional free-energy profiles from the MFPT and steady-state distribution measured along a reaction coordinate, but conventional implementations become inefficient for sufficiently high barriers because spontaneous crossings are rarely observed. We introduce a "top-start" extension that initiates trajectories near the barrier top and reconstructs the free-energy profile from their subsequent evolution away from the barrier toward lower-free-energy regions. We establish the equivalence between the top-start and two-region constructions using a Markov-chain transition-matrix formulation. We validate the method using one-dimensional random-walk simulations across low, medium, and high free-energy barriers, with transition-matrix calculations providing an exact benchmark for the corresponding discretized models. The top-start reconstruction remains accurate in the high-barrier regime where conventional MFPT sampling becomes prohibitively inefficient.
authors: Ying Jiang, Ivan Saika-Voivod
title: Extending the mean first-passage-time formalism to the reconstruction of high free-energy barriers: A top-start approach

abstract: Understanding why 2D materials remain suspended in solutions is essential to understanding the mechanisms of aggregation and exfoliation. These dynamics have been difficult to model because of the long timescales and large activation energies involved in these simulations. Here we describe an improved strategy for modelling the solvation and stability of 2D materials that uses the Gibbs free energy of solvation to accurately calibrate two disconnected potential energy surfaces for the fully desolvated and fully solvated 2D materials. By joining these surfaces using solvation energy, we obtain predictions for 2D material stability in various solvents that are qualitatively different than prior simulations and that have excellent agreement with experimental results. Our approach predicts a much higher barrier to full desolvation of the material, suggesting that materials that appear to be aggregated in fact still retain monolayers of solvent between adjacent layers of 2D materials. This work provides much needed understanding on the interactions between the solvent and 2D material that can guide future experimental work.
authors: Lindsey N. Ioos, Duncan A. Peterson, Scott C. Warren
title: Quantitative Modelling of Solvation in 2D Materials via Alchemical Decoupling and Potential Energy Surfaces

abstract: We examine how the Curie--Weiss cell fluid model can be quantitatively related to real fluids by determining its microscopic parameters from experimental critical-point data for water, carbon dioxide, and three polyol ester lubricants (POE5, POE7, and POE9). The microscopic parameters of the model are determined from the experimental values of the critical temperature and critical density: the global attraction coupling constant is fixed by the critical temperature, and the cell volume by the critical density. The critical pressure then follows as an independent model prediction, deviating from experimental values by 10--41$\%$ across the studied substances. Varying the ratio of local repulsion to global attraction $f=J_2/J_1$ over a wide range has only a weak effect on this deviation. For $f\geq1$, the model's critical compressibility factor lays within a narrow range $Z_c\approx0.382-0.386$, remaining close to the mean-field van der Waals value $Z_c=3/8=0.375$ and consistently overestimating experimental values. The best agreement with experiment is obtained for the polyol ester lubricants and improves along the POE5--POE7--POE9 series with increasing molar mass, suggesting that multiple-occupancy cell fluid models are well suited to systems of large molecules, particularly soft-matter systems with bounded interaction potentials. We further show that generalizing the model by introducing a temperature- and phase-dependent effective attraction allows it to describe a triple point and to reproduce the broad range of critical-to-triple temperature ratios $T_c/T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ characteristic of real fluids.
authors: I. V. Pylyuk, O. A. Dobush, M. P. Kozlovskii, R. V. Romanik, M. A. Shpot
title: Curie-Weiss cell fluid model: Fitting to experimental critical-point data

abstract: Living supramolecular materials such as microtubules and actin filaments assemble and function in dynamic, heterogeneous environments, subject to chemical concentration gradients. Their rapid and precise response to such gradients---via aggregation, disassembly, or autonomous motion---underlies the fine spatiotemporal control typical of living systems. Reproducing such responsiveness in synthetic materials is a central challenge in materials science and requires a molecular-level understanding of how gradients couple to supramolecular structure and dynamics, which remains difficult to access experimentally. To this end, we combine implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) with the constant chemical potential MD (C$μ$MD) technique to investigate, at molecular resolution, the coupling of two prototypical supramolecular polymer models with externally imposed ionic concentration gradients. Despite their contrasting responses to homogeneous ionic conditions, both systems undergo pronounced spatial reorganization under the gradient, generating regions of locally enhanced supramolecular activity that are inaccessible to homogeneous systems with the same overall content of self-assembling species. Crucially, the local supramolecular dynamics is largely determined by the local concentrations, consistent with the formation of local quasi-equilibria: this direct connection between spatial composition and supramolecular activity emerges as a common governing principle across the two models. These findings shed light on the spatially complex supramolecular response that can be triggered by chemical gradients, and show how a single gradient simulation can encode this response across a continuous range of local chemical environments, thus providing a general strategy to investigate and design materials operating under spatially heterogeneous conditions.

abstract: Development of computational models for single-channel patch-clamp analysis is hampered by limited availability of labelled (idealised) data. Since experiment alone cannot provide a genuine ground truth, two simulation methods are commonly employed; Stochastic sampling from a specified Markov model, augmented with synthetic noise allows creation of unlimited, flawlessly idealised/annotated datasets, yet its authenticity hinges entirely on the premises underlying data and noise generation. A more recent method uses GAN-based generation, this also replicates real-world noise and artefacts, but does not include a ground truth idealisation or annotation and training is notoriously unstable. Here, we introduce DiffuChannel, a conditional noise-removal diffusion model that addresses these drawbacks. Channel dynamics come directly from a user-defined discrete-time Markov chain (or a model fitted to biological seed data), thus, the state assignment for each synthetic trace is precisely determined by design. The diffusion model is then trained exclusively to capture the noise distribution of raw current conditioned on a given idealisation, thereby replicating genuine noise, filtering, and artefact patterns observed in real data without needing to hand craft noise models. We use a two-step coarse-to-fine workflow that starts with a defined slow-envelope component conditioned on longer-term dwell-time features extracted from the input idealisation. This allows a degree of baseline drift and time-dependent relaxations to be captured over timescales far longer than the network's field of view. At generation time, we use a context-preserving inpainting method that enables creation of relatively seamless traces of any desired duration. We demonstrate that with only a limited set of labelled seed traces, synthetic records yield realistic all-points amplitude distribution, noise power spectrum, autocorrelation pattern, and slow envelope comparable to the source data. The model achieves a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between windowed real and generated data of 0.005 (median across the five phenotypes). This compares to a within real-split-half MMD value of 0.002 and an amplitude-matched white noise MMD value of 0.108. In this paper, we benchmark this against DeepGANnel. Since the underlying Markov model is defined rather than estimated, DiffuChannel generates infinite, perfectly labelled, phenotype-consistent training data ideal for developing and testing idealisation algorithms. We find that, in practice, this new method is far more stable than previous GAN models and runs start to end without human intervention. We provide the model open-source along with an interactive web-based training and synthesis interface/app.

abstract: Ion permeation in the two-pore-domain K+ (K2P) channel TREK1 is gated largely at the selectivity filter (SF), by a C-type-like inactivation mechanism involving distortions of the SF structure; and by a carbonyl flip, which disrupts K+ coordination. Both are prevented by a small-molecule activator bound adjacent to the SF, in a site termed the modulator pocket; yet which pocket regions carry the binding signal, and whether they couple to gating, is unclear. We use 46 chemical substitutions on the activator ML335, evaluated by non-equilibrium alchemical free-energy calculations, as an affinity perturbation scan on the lower- and upper pocket. The response is strongly asymmetric: Lower-ring substitutions impair binding, which we trace to a {pi}-{pi} stacking network connecting the M3, P2, P1 helices, and the SF. Conversely, upper-ring substitutions are tolerated and reshape contacts with the Cap-P1 and SF2-M4 loops; and with the upper SF. The identified affinity hotspots overlap with residues independently implicated in TREK gating by external cues such as pH, temperature, pressure, and cytosolic-sensor transduction, suggesting that high-affinity pocket sites might also shape the gating landscape.

abstract: Deriving sequential information from complex sounds is a challenge for auditory systems, yet it remains unclear whether humans and nonhuman species integrate multidimensional cues or prioritize a single dimension when processing multidimensional input. We investigated how humans and zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) process concurrent acoustic cues using an identical behavioural paradigm with complex-tone sequences. By presenting probe stimuli that selectively preserved or disrupted either pitch or formant trajectory, we quantified these processing strategies. We show that zebra finches employ an additive integration strategy, treating pitch and formant trajectories as complementary components of a unified auditory pattern. In contrast, humans exhibit a dominant reliance on pitch. Experience further modulates this bias, with trained human listeners recruiting secondary cues to preserve learned relational structure when pitch is unreliable. These findings imply a cross-species divergence in auditory representation, suggesting that auditory processing is shaped by an interplay of species-specific priorities and experience-dependent functional substitution.

abstract: RIG-I is an innate immune receptor for viral double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Upon binding dsRNA, RIG-I nucleates MAVS filaments through its two caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD). However, how the 2CARD behaves during activation has remained unclear. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy, we visualized the 2CARD in full-length RIG-I across its apo, dsRNA-bound, translocating, multimeric, and polyubiquitin-bound states. Protrusions consistent with the 2CARD appeared only transiently in the apo state, whereas a mobile 2CARD emerged upon RNA binding. During ATP-driven translocation, wild-type RIG-I moved approximately twofold slower and showed more frequent pauses and multimers than RIG-I {Delta}2CARD. Within multimers, 2CARDs formed a complex that polyubiquitin stabilized into larger, dsRNA-deforming assemblies. These findings reveal the 2CARD as a brake on the RIG-I motor, beyond signaling.

abstract: Human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) is a neglected tropical disease transmitted by infected tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) in sub-Saharan Africa. Infected tsetse flies can transmit trypanosomes, including Trypanosoma brucei subspecies that cause HAT in humans, as well as other trypanosome species that cause animal African trypanosomiasis in domestic animals and infect wildlife. Tsetse flies feed on a broad spectrum of hosts, including humans, elephants, buffaloes, rhinos, hippos, turtles, and monitor lizards. To understand how the insects can penetrate such diverse skin types, we detailed the anatomical structures involved in tsetse blood feeding, their mechanical properties, and the forces exerted by the fly during probing. We found that the tsetse fly’s feeding apparatus does not rely on exceptionally unique structures or extraordinary forces. Instead, the tsetse fly has evolved subtle yet highly efficient adaptations, which include a labellum equipped with arrays of small teeth. When combined with a robust retraction movement of the proboscis, these structures create lesions on various types of skin, thus facilitating blood pool feeding on a broad host spectrum.

abstract: Hereditary stomatocytosis (HSt) comprises red blood cell (RBC) disorders characterized by cup-shaped erythrocytes that share a nominal morphology yet respond oppositely to splenectomy: the procedure is often curative in overhydrated HSt (OHS) and intermediate phenotypes but can precipitate life-threatening thromboembolism in dehydrated HSt (DHS/xerocytosis). This “splenectomy paradox” persists because clinicians cannot predict which patients will benefit. A central obstacle is that RBC biomechanics is governed by several partly independent parameters—membrane shear modulus (μ), bending rigidity (kc), surface-to-volume ratio (S/V), and cytoplasmic viscosity (ηcyto)—that existing assays capture only piecemeal.

abstract: Soft, porous materials combine elasticity with fluid transport, yet how these properties interact to produce mechanical instabilities remains poorly understood. Here we use polyacrylamide microbeads and microcapsules as model of soft porous materials to investigate this coupling. By combining quantitative micropipette aspiration with scaling analysis, we establish a relationship between elastic modulus E and hydraulic permeability k, showing that both are governed by the network mesh size even in highly heterogeneous gels. In hollow microcapsules, we observe buckling instabilities within well-defined ranges of shell thickness and pipette radius. A model coupling shell elasticity to hydrodynamically driven deswelling accounts for these instabilities and reveals how solvent transport can trigger mechanical collapse. These results establish a direct link between network structure, fluid transport and mechanical instability, providing a framework for understanding similar phenomena in physical gels, biological vesicles and shell-coated condensates, with potential relevance to cellular mechanics, tissue engineering and adaptive materials.

abstract: Understanding the mechanisms underlying substrate recognition and selectivity is essential for developing new biotechnological applications of carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs). Many members of CBM family 2 (CBM2) prefer binding to crystalline substrates and show diverse substrate specificities despite sharing similar folds. We show here that CBM2 specificity cannot be rationalized solely based on sequence and fold. Rather, specific binding of CBM2s to crystalline surfaces depends on a balance of topological complementarity, hydrophobic dehydration, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. We compare the binding modes of ScCBM2 and BaCBM2 on cellulose, chitin, and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) with respect to protein and substrate properties. Using MD simulations and NMR, we explore the CBMs' surface topology, hydration, solvent accessibility, and electrostatics. The results indicate that the two CBMs may bind to crystalline substrates in opposite orientations, and that the interplay between hydrophobic and {pi}-stacking interactions along the aromatic triad and hydrogen-bonding interactions on either side determines their orientation. We further show that higher water density at the aromatic triad correlates with higher substrate affinity. Lastly, we probe the interaction dynamics of BaCBM2 with PET nanoparticles and the monomer bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) using NMR relaxation and solvent paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (sPRE) experiments, revealing a mixture of transient, low-population states involved in PET binding. These insights clarify the interplay among factors that drive CBM2 substrate recognition and highlight the importance of evaluating surface hydration and protein dynamics in future CBM2 studies.

title: Decoding CBM2 binding modes: how similar folds achieve distinct substrate preferences

abstract: Quantitative fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is limited by a lack of probes that combine single-residue specificity, minimal steric perturbation, visible-light excitation, and strong environment-dependent lifetime contrast. We introduce benzodiazole-based non-canonical amino acids (BD-ncAAs) as compact, genetically encoded sensors for site-specific FLIM. Using an engineered pyrrolysyl-tRNA synthetase pair, we incorporate three different BD-ncAAs into proteins in living cells. Site-specific incorporation of BD-ncAAs into a nanobody at different positions preserved native structure and antigen binding. The lead probe, cyano-substituted CBDS, exhibits visible-light excitation, large Stokes shifts, and pronounced environment-dependent fluorescence lifetimes spanning 1 to 24 ns. Under wash-free, live-cell FLIM conditions, CBDS quantitatively resolves localized structural microenvironments and transmembrane hydration gradients, while also distinguishing distinct states during protein secretion in eukaryotes. BD-ncAAs present genetically encoded, minimally perturbing reporters for tracking target proteins, detecting interactions with binding partners, and quantifying site-specific solvent accessibility in living cells by quantitative FLIM.

abstract: Ser195 is highly conserved as the catalytic nucleophile in trypsin like serine proteases, yet the molecular basis for the strong preference for serine over the chemically similar threonine residue remains unclear. Here, we used well tempered metadynamics and microsecond long molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the conformational energetics of S195 and T195 in thrombin. Well tempered metadynamics revealed distinct rotameric free energy landscapes in both the apo and the ligand bound systems. In the apo state, S195 preferentially occupied a lower angle rotameric state, while T195 exhibited two low energy states with similar free energies. Unbiased simulations further showed greater conformational heterogeneity and increased higher angle sampling for T195. Evaluation of the His57 to residue 195 hydrogen bond further revealed that S195 maintained close hydrogen bond distances across both rotameric regions, whereas T195 exhibited longer and more variable His57 to hydroxyl distances with reduced distance based occupancy. Analysis of the local environment showed that the additional T195 methyl group was associated with redistributed protein contacts. Additional rotamer conditioned analyses demonstrated differences in local packing within corresponding conformational states. Furthermore, solvent accessibility and water contact analyses revealed that the effects of the substitution on the catalytic side chain environment depend on rotameric conformation. Together, these findings demonstrate that two complementary simulation approaches converge on similar conformational preferences and suggest that the S195T substitution alters the rotameric free energy landscape in association with changes in catalytic geometry, local packing, and solvation. These results provide insight into the evolutionary preference for serine over threonine at the catalytic position of thrombin.

abstract: A systematic study on structurally similar, spectrally distinguishable dual-mode pH sensors (1) with red–blue and (2) with red–green emission is presented covering optical spectroscopic measurements in solution and in HeLa cells and their sensing performance is compared. As determined from their emission and excitation spectra, dual-mode sensors 1 and 2 exhibit a broad range of pKa values, including four different pKa for 2 calculated by the ratiometric emission intensities in the neutral to acidic pH range. abstract: We investigated the behaviour of freshwater blackworms (\emph{Lumbriculus variegatus}) in a circular maze containing food in its central chamber. Registered occupancy maps revealed non-uniform use of corridors and chambers. Because the study did not include a no-food control, the observations demonstrate central-chamber entry and spatial exploration but do not by themselves establish food localisation or chemotaxis. The assay provides a reproducible framework for studying annelid exploration and for future controlled comparisons of sensory cues and maze complexity.

abstract: Photoacoustic sensing has emerged as a promising technique for detecting polymeric particles suspended in liquids through the conversion of absorbed optical energy into acoustic signals. Here, we present a multiscale computational study of the photoacoustic response of polystyrene (PS) beads suspended in water under pulsed optical excitation. The framework combines particle-resolved simulations of individual beads with point-particle descriptions of randomly distributed multi-particle suspensions. The results reveal a rapid acoustic transient followed by a residual pressure field persisting in the liquid. As particle concentration increases, the residual pressure level progressively rises and exhibits an approximately square-root dependence on the number of photoacoustic sources. The point-particle study further shows that the pressure response is closely related to the effective number of irradiated particles rather than to the nominal suspension concentration, while the induced particle motion remains negligible. Overall, the present results provide a physically grounded basis for interpreting photoacoustic signals from PS bead suspensions in water and support future developments of photoacoustic sensing strategies for applications ranging from microplastic detection in aqueous media to polymer-bead-based microfluidic and bioanalytical platforms.

abstract: Cavitation influences the failure of elastomers and soft adhesives, but connecting its microscopic initiation to subsequent cavity growth remains challenging. Here, we develop a discrete mesoscale framework that combines finitely extensible, breakable strands with local van der Waals interactions to examine how cohesion and network heterogeneity transform distributed dilation into localized damage. In the simulations, local cohesive instability produces a network-scale precursor whose subsequent expansion is coupled to strand stretching and rupture. Cohesive strength and intrinsic defect size govern the critical hydrostatic tension, while cohesion also controls the number and spatial distribution of cavities. Under confined loading, decreasing the layer thickness promotes multiple cavities and distributed strand rupture, extending the load-bearing response and increasing the critical work density of rupture. An energetic interpretation based on the thickness dependence of the crack-driving force connects these observations to competition between additional cavity nucleation and propagation of existing damage. The results link local cohesive instability to the collective evolution of cavities and rupture in disordered polymer networks.

abstract: By modulating the orientation of a uniform magnetic field it is possible to transport magnetic microparticles above magnetic patterns. In periodic patterns, driving control loops that wind around special orientations, which are dictated by the symmetry of the pattern, induce transport by one unit cell. The transport is topologically protected with trajectories controlled by the winding numbers of the control loop around the special orientations. In non-periodic patterns, the special orientations are position dependent, precluding a global characterization of the transport using a small set of winding numbers. We use here a reinforcement learning agent trained with Brownian dynamics simulation data that uses the local environment of the magnetic pattern to decide an action over the control loop. The agent autonomously discovers topological transport protocols directly from the particle response without prior characterization of the magnetic potential landscape. An agent trained solely on a complex non-periodic pattern directly generalizes to completely unseen periodic, quasicrystalline, and disordered substrates. Moreover, the agent dynamically adjusts the control loop to transport particles across lattice defects and to counterbalance external drift forces that would cause static topological loops to fail. By adding a pathfinding algorithm to the model, we additionally achieve simultaneous, independent transport of multiple identical colloids along different on demand trajectories. We demonstrate that the control loops can be directly transferred to an experimental setup to successfully drive magnetic microparticles across a non-uniform magnetic thin film.

abstract: We investigate how the translational motion of a compact skyrmion cluster can be converted into collective rotation through interactions with a periodic obstacle substrate. Using an effective particle model, we consider a seven-skyrmion cluster driven along a one-dimensional array of repulsive obstacle sites. For suitable obstacle spacings and interaction strengths, repeated interactions with the substrate produce coherent clockwise or counterclockwise rotation, giving rise to gear-like cluster dynamics. We characterize these states using the translational velocity, Hall angle, angular velocity, structural deformation, and a dimensionless gear ratio that relates cluster rotation to motion over the substrate periodicity. Dynamical phase diagrams identify rotating, nonrotating, wall-guided, transverse, and deformed regimes. We further show that coherent rotation persists in the overdamped limit, demonstrating that the conversion mechanism does not require an intrinsic Magnus force and may therefore extend to other driven cluster systems, including colloidal assemblies. These results provide a simple route for controlling collective rotation through structured substrates.

title: Skyrmion gears: translation-to-rotation conversion of skyrmion clusters along periodic substrates

abstract: We study the spontaneous motion and collective dynamics of self-phoretic particles on a ring. The particles act as localized sources of a chemical field, with particle-dependent source strengths, and respond to gradients of this field through particle-dependent phoretic mobilities. The chemical field undergoes diffusion and evaporation. For a single particle, we derive the exact threshold for spontaneous propulsion and establish the emergence of stable constant-velocity states near onset through a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. We then consider an active source coupled to a non-emitting tracer and determine the conditions for slipping and stable phase-locked motion. For two mutually coupled sources, the stationary antipodal configuration can lose stability through either a pitchfork or a Hopf bifurcation, depending on the relative source strengths and phoretic mobilities. We determine the competing instability thresholds and compare them with direct numerical simulations of the coupled particle-field equations. Beyond onset, the resulting translating and oscillatory states provide qualitative counterparts to modes of motion observed experimentally for camphor disks in annular water channels. These results connect the onset of individual propulsion, tracer entrainment, and collective motion within a common analytically tractable framework.

abstract: In artificial (micro)capsules or cells such as red blood cells for example, the two-dimensional (2D) rheology of the membrane (or the shell) is viscoelastic and not only elastic. The deformation and inclination of such a capsule are theoretically studied under shear and extensional flows. The membrane mechanics is described by the Kelvin-Voigt model: the 2D dissipation with the Boussinesq-Scriven law associated to specific dilational and shear Boussinesq numbers $Bq_d$ and $Bq_d$ respectively while the elastic constitutive law is either Hookean, strain-softening (neoHookean) or strain-hardening (Skalak). The dynamics depends on the elastic capillary number $Ca$, the Poisson ratio (or $C$ in Skalak law), the viscosity ratio $λ$, the nonlinearities included in the constitutive law and both boussinesq numbers. Three dynamics are identified in the limit of weak deformations: a tank-treading motion in the limit of small elastic capillary number with a characteristic time depending on $λ$, $Bq_s$ and $Bq_d$, an oscillation without any elasticity and a damped oscillation leading to a tank-treading motion in the limit of large Boussinesq numbers. In all cases, both shear and dilational 2D dissipations contribute differently leading to non-trivial results. In the case of a Skalak law with $C=1$, $Bq=Bq_s=Bq_d$ and $Bq>>λ$, the deformations in the limits $Ca<<1$, $Bq=O(1)$ and $Ca=O(1)$, $Bq>>1$ determined in the seminal work of \cite{barthes1985role} are recovered.
authors: Paul Regazzi, Marc Leonetti
title: Impact of shear and dilational membrane viscosities on capsule shape and dynamics under shear flow: a theoretical study

abstract: Colloidal suspensions that are confined between two closely spaced plates and left to evaporate slowly form maze-like labyrinth patterns in the final stage of evaporation. The fingers in these patterns form bifurcations and occasionally loops, which we may quantify with a skeletonization method. We compare drying patterns formed with two different salt concentrations in the droplet which changes the screening length and therefore the effective colloid interactions. We find that the junctions generally follow Murray's law for optimal transport networks, and that the typical bifurcation angles peak around 53. Screened droplets additionally show more loopy networks, and is characterized by bands of transversal fingers before merging into a central non-fingering colloidal aggregate. Our observations suggest that colloid-colloid interactions can strongly influence the large-scale topology of the pattern while leaving the local geometry of the individual fingers unchanged.
authors: Andreas Andersen Hennig, Natalia Kizilova, Ilaria Beechey-Newman, Erika Eiser
title: Colloid-Colloid Interactions Impact Network Morphology of Confined Colloidal Drying Patterns

abstract: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $Ω(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.
authors: Russell Kajouri, Adyant Agrawal, Philipp Stärk, Alexander Schlaich, Christian Holm
title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling

abstract: Active gels are intrinsically non-equilibrium materials whose structural and dynamical heterogeneity emerges from the interplay of attractive interactions, thermal fluctuations, and self-propulsion. We investigate a model active gel, simulated using large-scale Brownian dynamics simulations, to explore the effects of temperature $T$, active force strength $f_0$, persistence timescale $τ_p$, and active particle concentration $ρ_a$. We characterize the structure of the evolving gel network through morphological analysis, while dynamical changes are quantified by the relaxation timescale and dynamical heterogeneity (DH). We show that an optimal choice of activity parameters yields a percolating gel network with faster gelation and larger voids and clusters, enhancing mechanical stability. Conversely, the structural relaxation timescale and DH decrease with increasing activity, indicating enhanced particle rearrangements and reduced spatial correlations of mobile and immobile regions. An effective temperature ($T_\text{eff}$) framework for colloidal gels maps structural quantities and relaxation timescales in an active gel onto those of a passive gel. More interestingly, the growth of DH with increasing swim force can also be described by the same effective-temperature framework, in stark contrast to observations in active glasses. Our findings show that, in colloidal gels, temperature and active force compete, giving rise to similar structural ordering and, consequently, similar DH at the same $T_\text{eff}$. These findings highlight the crucial role of structural ordering in governing DH in active colloidal gels, as compared to active glasses.
authors: Santu Nath, Sudipta Mandal, Smarajit Karmakar
title: Activity-Induced Structural and Dynamical Heterogeneity in Colloidal Gels

abstract: The yielding of amorphous solids has been extensively studied in the athermal limit, but the influence of thermal fluctuations is much less understood, in particular for glasses of different stability. Using molecular dynamics simulations of a model glass where the swap Monte Carlo algorithm can be employed, we study the yield stress at finite temperature and shear rate, both in steady flow and at shear start-up, over a broad range of glass stability. Thermal fluctuations soften both the dynamic yield stress in steady state and the start-up yield stress. In all cases, the temperature dependence is compatible with the $T^{2/3}$ law expected for thermally activated yielding near a saddle-node instability, with no systematic dependence of the exponent on stability or shear rate. Extrapolations to zero temperature recover the athermal yield stresses. The amplitude of the softening at start-up, by contrast, depends strongly on stability: highly stable glasses are much less sensitive to temperature than poorly annealed ones. A description of yielding at finite temperature must therefore account explicitly for the stability of the glass.
authors: Tianze Wan, Ludovic Berthier
title: Thermal softening of the yield stress in glasses with different stability

abstract: Adaptive search and travel strategies enable biological swimmers to explore complex environments, but remain difficult to encode in minimal synthetic microswimmers. Here, we unveil multiple dynamical and orientational states of rod-like Janus microswimmers actuated via electric fields: planar active, oriented chiral and persistent rods. We discover a hidden dynamical state after pre-orienting them, which allows us to switch on demand from strong chiral to persistent motion. We harness this phenomenological orientation and chirality switch for exploration in microstructured porous arrays. Here, strong chirality promotes local scanning but drives circular trapping and poor net displacement, whereas the pre-aligned dynamical state enables efficient obstacle sorting, and trap escape. Comparing experiments with simulations of active Brownian particles in the very same experimentally-extracted obstacle geometries, we quantify navigation efficiency via first-passage time statistics, revealing how chirality tuning optimizes the trade-off between local exploration and long-range transport.

title: Dynamical-state switching controls active microrod navigation in porous media

abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using microfabricated 3D cancer–CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight cancer cell lines, three CAF populations, and heterotypic tumor–CAF assemblies, spanning nearly two orders of magnitude. Surface tension is first shown to govern spheroid morphology and modulate drug response. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Surface tension alone therefore fails to predict CAF organization. Instead, the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) state of cancer cells emerges as a major determinant: epithelial-like tumors promote CAF core accumulation, whereas mesenchymal-like states favor persistent mixing. Peripheral CAF localization emerges only under restricted conditions combining high tumor cohesion and sequential stromal recruitment. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor–stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.
authors: Claire Wilhelm
title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm

abstract: Originally coined 100 years ago to represent a shear-reversible sol-gel transition, the range of the term "thixotropy" has gradually expanded to encompass time-dependent changes in viscosity. Since this risks confusing "thixotropy" with ordinary nonlinear viscoelastic behavior, in this work we seek simple, historically faithful, quantifiable, and experimentally testable definitions of "thixotropy" that avoid this confusion. By analysing both historical tradition and published experimental data, we arrive at three complementary definitions. Definition 0 provides an idealized, purely inelastic reference useful primarily for recognizing thixotropy in a constitutive equation. Definitions 1 and 2, which are more practical, require, respectively, unusually large strains to reach steady state, and unbounded growth of the material relaxation time during rest. Definition 1 can apply in either shear-rate or stress-controlled modes, with the latter encompassing the so-called "viscosity bifurcation." These criteria are tested across diverse materials that we identify as thixotropic based on their responses clearly exceeding their viscoelastic reference scales. The framework is deliberately phenomenological and does not require specific microscopic mechanisms, allowing diverse materials to be described within a common rheological language, as is typical for rheological terminology. We believe that these definitions provide a practical framework for assigning thixotropy a more definite place in rheological taxonomy.
authors: Yogesh M. Joshi, Ronald G. Larson
title: Defining Thixotropy

abstract: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics.   We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development.   Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.
authors: Louisa Cornelis, Haewon Jeong, Irina Espejo, Payel Mukhopadhyay
title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos

abstract: Active matter systems composed of self-propelled entities exhibit a wide range of out-of-equilibrium phase behaviors and collective dynamics. Assemblies of active particles, e.g., in a linear structure, are particularly interesting, as they exhibit an intriguing interplay between activity and geometrical restrictions due to self-avoidance and entanglements. Using Langevin dynamics simulations of an active Brownian ring polymer with translational and rotational inertia, we uncover an inertia-driven re-entrant coil-globule transition in the absence of any attractive interactions. We show that rotational inertia plays a paramount role, leading, in the globular state, to spontaneous, nonzero, radially outward polarization of the active forces. Self-avoidance and entanglements break the rotational symmetry of active beads and effectively stabilize the globular states. The transition becomes increasingly sharp with increasing rotational inertia, yielding highly compact globular conformations at intermediate activities, whereas at high activity the polymer re-expands into a coil state. Scaling of the radius of gyration reveals crossovers from self-avoiding, phantom-like to compact-globular structures. Further, rotational inertia enhances transport properties, with an intermediate activity-induced Rouse-type bead diffusion and a long-time diffusion coefficient displaying a power-law dependence on the moment of inertia. Our study establishes a purely inertia-induced mechanism for controlling the collapse of active polymers, arising from spontaneous active-force polarization and self-avoidance.
authors: Rakesh Palariya, Arindam Panda, Roland G. Winkler, Sunil P Singh
title: Self-Avoidance Governs Re-entrant Coil-Globule Transition of Inertial Active Brownian Ring Polymers

abstract: Despite a vigorous effort, a comprehensive and satisfactory understanding of the dynamics underlying the glass transition in finite-dimensional systems has not yet emerged. One key hallmark of supercooled liquids approaching the glass transition is the breakdown of the classical Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, manifested as the decoupling between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time, commonly described by a fractional SE relation. Whether and how the fractional SE exponents vary remains an ongoing debate, even for the simplest supercooled liquids. In this work, we numerically establish a universal relation between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time by introducing characteristic scales that are revealed under the condition of constant dynamical heterogeneity. Moreover, this universal relation could also capture literature data for supercooled water and silica. Remarkably, we find that the fractional SE exponent is invariant across various supercooled liquids studied spanning a wide range of fragility, thereby challenging the prevailing view that the fractional SE exponent is correlated with fragility. Our study demonstrates that investigating dynamical heterogeneity yields more valuable insights into understanding glassy dynamics than expected.
authors: Mingyu Zhu, Xinyu Chang, Licun Fu, Yiming Zheng, Lijin Wang
title: Universal link between structural relaxation and self-diffusion in simple supercooled liquids

abstract: Models of curvature-driven membrane sorting couple composition directly to membrane bending elasticity. Here we show that shape deformations can destabilize a homogeneous state without this composition-dependent mechanical coupling. We analyze the eigenspectrum of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on deformed spheres analytically, and verify it numerically. As the deformation amplitude increases, the spectral degeneracy breaks, and the lowest nonzero eigenvalue decreases substantially. Using Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, we show that this eigenvalue softening provides a purely geometric route to phase separation.
authors: Avraham Moriel, Howard A. Stone
title: Deformation-induced spectral softening drives phase separation on non-spherical membranes

abstract: Microscopy is foundational to biology, enabling direct observation of otherwise inaccessible cellular structures and processes. Artificial intelligence has advanced microscopy through acquisition control, image analysis, and natural language instrument operation. No system has unified these steps into a complete experimental loop. We introduce an autonomous multi-agent system that turns plain language goals into measurements and statistically tested answers, gating and executing every action in deterministic code. This sets the groundwork for extending microscopy from biological observation to autonomous investigation.
authors: Nieves Vasquez, W. E.; Lin, J.; Azukas, J.; Yang, E.; Hu, C.-K.; Ma, T.; Carlini, L.
title: GENIE: a multi-agent system for closed-loop autonomous microscopy

abstract: Identifying synthetically accessible, potent ligands from vast chemical space remains a major challenge in drug discovery, particularly because experimental synthesis and testing are costly and low throughput. Here, we present a fully open-source computational-experimental workflow that integrates fragment-based de novo molecular design with rigorous alchemical absolute binding free-energy calculations to enable physics-based prioritization before chemical synthesis. We apply this strategy by targeting the virulence-associated zinc metalloprotease LasB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. From ~40,000 diverse compounds generated through multi-objective optimization, a small subset was prioritized and experimentally evaluated, leading to the discovery of three previously unreported nanomolar inhibitors (IC50 22-53 nM) with excellent metabolic and plasma stability. This work demonstrates a general and scalable framework for coupling generative molecular design with quantitative binding affinity prediction, improving decision-making and reducing the cost, time, and risk associated with early-stage drug discovery.
authors: Martinez Leon, A.; Vgenopoulou, A.; Jezequel, G.; Kany, A. M.; Hirsch, A. K.; Hub, J. S.
title: Prospective discovery of LasB inhibitors by integrating generative design, free energy ranking, and experimental validation

abstract: Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) is widely used to assess protein thermal stability and to compare protein variants, ligands, or formulations with limited sample consumption. Yet, the reproducibility of DSF derived parameters across laboratories, instruments and analysis workflows remains poorly defined. Here, we report a two phase interlaboratory benchmark using a shared VHH sample across 26 laboratories, 28 instruments and seven DSF instrument models. In Phase 1, participants applied their routine acquisition and analysis workflows, whereas in Phase 2, acquisition conditions were harmonised. Datasets were analysed locally and then centrally reprocessed with MoltenProt. Participant reported apparent melting temperatures (Tm) showed good within instrument repeatability but moderate inter instrument dispersion. Harmonisation of acquisition conditions did not substantially reduce this dispersion. Conversely, centralised reprocessing narrowed the distribution among retained datasets, indicating contributions from analysis workflows and data acceptance criteria in addition to instrument dependent factors. Comparison with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) further showed that apparent Tm depended strongly on the fluorescence readout. For this VHH, single wavelength fluorescence at 350 nm showed the closest agreement with the DSC transition temperature, whereas the 350/330 nm ratio and barycentric mean generally yielded higher values. Furthermore, DSF derived apparent unfolding enthalpies were more variable than apparent Tm. Together, these findings show that DSF can be highly repeatable within a defined instrument and workflow, but that quantitative comparability across instruments depends on instrument specific effects, the choice of fluorescence readout and analysis strategy. Improved comparability will require transparent reporting of acquisition and analysis conditions, explicit data quality criteria, and well characterised reference materials to monitor instrument dependent offsets.

abstract: Although two-component systems (TCSs) play ubiquitous roles in sensing signals for bacterial survival and virulence, a detailed structural map of the signal transduction pathway is lacking. Bacteriophytochromes (BphPs) are enzymatic photoreceptors with homologs in plants that regulate bacterial physiological responses via TCS signaling. Here, we employ cryo-EM to elucidate the structural basis of a light-regulated TCS by capturing the full-length BphP histidine kinase (HK) in complex with its downstream response regulator (RR). The RR binds as a dimer to the HK but contacts the enzyme only through one subunit. Light absorption perturbs the entire BphP structure, including the HK domain, which disrupts phosphorylation and phosphotransfer reactions and promote TCS complex dissociation. Thus, light controls signaling through both HK activity and reversible binding of the RR.

abstract: Branched antimicrobial peptides offer a promising strategy for improving the stability and activity of membrane-active peptides, but how branching alters self-association and membrane binding remains unclear. We used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to compare tetra-branched SET-M33 with its linear branch sequence Q33 (KKIRVRLSA) in water and at an anionic bacterial-membrane model, to do this, systems containing equivalent numbers of Q33 sequence units were simulated. Q33 formed dimers and higher-order oligomers, particularly at the membrane interface and under hydration-tuned enhanced sampling. In contrast, SET-M33 remained more dispersed, as the branched scaffold and its high cationic charge limited peptide-peptide association while allowing multivalent membrane binding. Both architectures associated rapidly with the bilayer but remained predominantly surface-bound, without persistent pore formation or complete insertion. Q33 showed stronger membrane-induced helical stabilization, whereas SET-M33 retained a more heterogeneous conformational ensemble. Overall, branching primarily altered lateral peptide organization while preserving close membrane association, suppressing uncontrolled self-aggregation and providing an atomistic rationale for the distinct behavior of SET-M33 relative to Q33.
authors: Satvati, S.; Rigoli, M.; Fortuna, S.; Falciani, C.; Pini, A.; Rocchia, W.
title: Branching Suppresses Self-Aggregation while Preserving Membrane Association in SET-M33: An Atomistic Molecular Dynamics Study

abstract: Ligands that bind to the same G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) can produce widely different levels of signaling. These differences in efficacy are central to pharmacology, yet how a receptor sequence determines signaling level remains incompletely understood. Here we develop a deep mutational pharmacology approach to measure how each residue in the -opioid receptor (OR) shapes responses to 15 opioids, yielding ~400,000 measurements of variant effects on signaling and expression, including full concentration-response series for three agonists. Mutational effects on potency are strongest near the orthosteric pocket, whereas effects on efficacy extend through the transmembrane core and intracellular face. Ligands share many functional determinants, but sensitivity to mutation differs with efficacy. As efficacy decreases, the residues required for signaling shift from the binding pocket towards the intracellular face; partial agonists therefore depend on residues that are dispensable for full agonists. Mutations can broadly increase receptor responses, allowing antagonists such as naloxone to produce signaling comparable to a full agonist and increasing the efficacy of partial agonist ligands. Combined mutations can also reorder the relative efficacies of ligands, showing that sequence changes reshape pharmacological differences rather than simply increasing or decreasing all responses together. These findings support a model in which ligands of different efficacy activate the receptor through distinct allosteric mechanisms which are determined by residues distributed across the receptor. Mapping these contributions across diverse ligands with deep mutational pharmacology provides a way to understand how one receptor converts molecular recognition into a range of signaling outputs.
